content.title: What is the penalty for filing taxes late? How to ask for an extension
content.text: Today is the deadline for filing federal income taxes in the United States.Scott Olson/Getty ImagesIf you’re still procrastinating your tax return, the clock is working against you. At midnight Wednesday, the federal filing deadline will pass — and missing it can get expensive, fast.April 15 — Tax Day — is a hard cutoff: returns must be filed by 11:59 p.m. local time to be considered on time by the IRS. Taxpayers living outside the United States and Puerto Rico on April 15 receive an automatic two-month extension to file their 2025 returns, moving the deadline to June 15.Article continues below this adGet Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.ONLY 25¢If that deadline passes and you haven’t filed, what happens next depends largely on whether you owe money and how quickly you respond.Failure-to-file vs. failure-to-pay penaltiesThe most immediate consequence is a failure-to-file penalty, which is typically steeper than the penalty for failing to pay.The IRS generally charges 5% of unpaid taxes for each month, or part of a month, that a return is late, up to a maximum of 25%.Article continues below this adFor taxpayers who owe and don’t pay by the deadline, a separate failure-to-pay penalty applies. That’s usually 0.5% of unpaid taxes per month, in addition to interest that accrues over time.Not everyone faces penalties. If you’re owed a refund, there’s no fee for filing late. However, returns must be filed within three years to claim a refund; after that, the money is forfeited.Should you still file if you can't afford to pay?Filing late is almost always better than not filing at all.Article continues below this adSubmitting your return — even without full payment — can significantly reduce penalties. Taxpayers facing financial hardship can explore options such as installment plans or temporary collection delays.Some taxpayers may have more time to file, but only if they planned ahead. Those who requested a filing extension before the deadline typically have until mid-October to submit their return.Extensions apply only to filing paperwork, not paying taxes owed. Any unpaid balance after April 15 can trigger penalties and interest.Article continues below this adAccording to the IRS, there are three ways to get an extension to file your tax return. Use Free File (no income limit for extensions): Use IRS Free File to electronically request an automatic tax-filing extension. Request an extension by mail: File Form 4868, Application for Automatic Extension of Time To File U.S. Individual Income Tax Return. You can file by mail, online with an IRS e-filing partner or through a tax professional. Estimate how much tax you owe for the year on the extension form: Subtract the taxes you already paid for the filing year. Pay online and check the box: Pay what you owe using an online payment option and check the box that you are paying as part of filing for an extension. You don’t have to file a separate extension form and you’ll receive a confirmation number of your extension for your records. — Marley Malenfant contributed reporting.Article continues below this adStories you won't want to miss, handpicked by Statesman editors.April 15, 2026Breaking & Trending ReporterJulianna Duennes Russ is a breaking and trending news reporter at the Austin American-Statesman.
